documents.content:
This page describes the approximate performance that Spanner can provide under optimal conditions, factors that can affect performance, and tips for testing and troubleshooting Spanner performance issues.

The information on this page applies to both GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL databases.

## Performance and storage improvements

Performance and storage improvements have rolled out to all [Spanner regional, dual-region, and multi-region instance configurations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/instance-configurations) . You don't need to make any changes to your application or manually configure anything in your Spanner instances to take advantage of these improvements, which are offered at no additional cost. These performance improvements result in higher throughput and better latency in Spanner nodes in all instance configurations.

### Increased performance throughput

All Spanner instance configurations have improved performance and offer increased throughput. The following table provides the approximate throughput (queries per second) for these Spanner instance configurations:

| Instance configuration type      | Peak reads (QPS per region) |        | Peak writes (QPS total) |     | Peak writes using [throughput optimized writes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/throughput-optimized-writes) (QPS total) |
|----------------------------------|-----------------------------|--------|-------------------------|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Regional**                     | SSD: 22,500 HDD: 1,500      | **or** | SSD: 3,500 HDD: 3,500   |     | SSD: 22,500 HDD: 22,500                                                                                                             |
| **Dual-region and multi-region** | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000      | **or** | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700   |     | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 15,000                                                                                                             |

For information about the performance throughput of these instance configurations, see [Performance for typical workloads](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/performance#typical-workloads) . For more information about using solid-state drives (SSD) and hard disk drives (HDD) to store your data, see [Tiered storage overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/tiered-storage) .

Read guidance is given per region (because reads can be served from any read-write or read-only region), while write guidance is for the entire configuration. Read guidance assumes you're reading single rows of 1KB. Write guidance assumes that you're writing single rows at 1KB of data per row.

You can achieve peak write performance with throughput optimized writes by setting a batching delay of 100 ms. For more information, see [Throughput optimized writes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/throughput-optimized-writes) .

In general, both the read and write throughputs of a Spanner instance scale linearly as you add more compute capacity (nodes or processing units) to the instance. For example, if a single-region Spanner instance with 2 nodes can provide up to 45,000 reads per second, then a single-region Spanner instance with 4 nodes can provide up to 90,000 reads per second.

If your Spanner workload doesn't achieve the expected performance, then see [troubleshooting query performance regressions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/troubleshooting-query-performance-regressions) for information about common causes.

### Increased storage

For all Spanner regional, dual-region, and multi-region instance configurations, each node (1,000 processing units) of compute capacity in the instance has an increased storage capacity of 10 TiB.

## Performance for typical workloads

All Spanner instance configurations have improved performance and offer increased throughput.

### Performance for regional configurations

Each 1,000 processing units (1 node) of compute capacity can provide the following peak performance (at 100% CPU) in a regional instance configuration:

| Peak reads (QPS per region) |        | Peak writes (QPS total) |     | Peak writes using [throughput optimized writes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/throughput-optimized-writes) (QPS total) |
|-----------------------------|--------|-------------------------|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| SSD: 22,500 HDD: 1,500      | **or** | SSD: 3,500 HDD: 3,500   |     | SSD: 22,500 HDD: 22,500                                                                                                             |

For regional instance configurations that support optional read-only replicas, each optional read-only replica provides an additional 7,500 reads per second for SSD storage and 500 reads per second for HDD storage.

> **Note:** These throughput numbers are **estimates only** , and they reflect a read-only or write-only workload. Spanner throughput is highly dependent on workload, schema design, and dataset characteristics. These throughput numbers can help as a starting point when you are estimating the approximate [compute capacity](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/compute-capacity) (nodes or processing units) required for your Spanner instance. But these numbers can't be used for exact sizing and cost estimates.

### Performance for dual-region configurations

Each 1,000 processing units (1 node) of compute capacity provides the following peak performance (at 100% CPU) in a dual-region instance configuration. To increase write throughput beyond the numbers in the table, use throughput optimized writes. For more information, see [Throughput optimized writes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/throughput-optimized-writes) .

| Base configuration name  | Approximate peak reads (QPS per region) | Approximate peak writes (QPS total) |
|--------------------------|-----------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| `dual-region-australia1` | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                  | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `dual-region-germany1`   | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                  | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `dual-region-india1`     | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                  | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `dual-region-japan1`     | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                  | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |

The read guidance applies per region because any region can serve reads, whereas the write guidance applies to the entire configuration. This guidance assumes that you read and write single rows at 1 KB of data per row.

### Performance for multi-region configurations

Each Spanner multi-region instance configuration has slightly different performance characteristics based on the replication topology. Use [throughput optimized writes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/throughput-optimized-writes) to increase write throughput beyond the numbers in the table.

Each 1,000 processing units (1 node) of compute capacity can provide the following peak performance (at 100% CPU):

| Base configuration name | Approximate peak reads (QPS per region)                                                                                                                                                                                          | Approximate peak writes (QPS total) |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| `asia1`                 | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `asia2`                 | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `eur3`                  | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `eur5`                  | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `eur6`                  | SSD: 15,000, 7,500 for each optional read-only replica HDD: 1,000, 500 for each optional read-only replica                                                                                                                       | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `eur7`                  | SSD: 15,000, 7,500 for each optional read-only replica HDD: 1,000, 500 for each optional read-only replica                                                                                                                       | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam3`                  | SSD: 15,000, 7,500 for each optional read-only replica HDD: 1,000, 500 for each optional read-only replica                                                                                                                       | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam6`                  | SSD: 15,000 in `us-central1` and `us-east1` 7,500 in `us-west1` and `us-west2` HDD: 1,000 in `us-central1` and `us-east1` 500 in `us-west1` and `us-west2` [*\[1\]*](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/performance#QPS) | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam7`                  | SSD: 15,000, 7,500 for each optional read-only replica HDD: 1,000, 500 for each optional read-only replica                                                                                                                       | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam8`                  | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam9`                  | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam10`                 | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam11`                 | SSD: 15,000, 7,500 for each optional read-only replica HDD: 1,000, 500 for each optional read-only replica                                                                                                                       | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam12`                 | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam13`                 | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam14`                 | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam15`                 | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam16`                 | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam-eur-asia1`         | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |
| `nam-eur-asia3`         | SSD: 15,000 HDD: 1,000                                                                                                                                                                                                           | SSD: 2,700 HDD: 2,700               |

- *\[1\]* : `us-west1` and `us-west2` provide only half of the QPS performance because they contain one replica per region instead of two.

The read guidance applies per region because any region can serve reads, whereas the write guidance applies to the entire configuration. This guidance assumes that you read and write single rows at 1 KB of data per row.

## Run your typical workloads against Spanner

Always run your own typical workloads against a Spanner instance when doing capacity planning, so you can figure out the best resource allocation for your applications. Google's PerfKit Benchmarker uses [YCSB](https://ycsb.site/) to benchmark cloud services. To create tests for your own workloads, follow the [PerfKitBenchmarker tutorial for Spanner](https://github.com/cloudspannerecosystem/spanner-benchmarks-tutorial) . When doing so, you should tune the parameters in the benchmarking configuration `yaml` files to make sure that the generated benchmark reflects the following characteristics in your production environment:

- Total size of your database
- Schema (for example, row key size, number of columns, and row data sizes)
- Data access pattern (row key distribution)
- Mixture of reads versus writes
- Type and complexity of queries

### Reproduce benchmark numbers

To reproduce the benchmark numbers, follow the [Benchmarking Spanner with PerfKit Benchmarker tutorial](https://github.com/cloudspannerecosystem/spanner-benchmarks-tutorial) using the corresponding `yaml` files in the [`throughput_benchmark`](https://github.com/cloudspannerecosystem/spanner-benchmarks-tutorial/tree/main/data/throughput_benchmarks) folder.

To benchmark instances in an instance configuration that has undergone [performance improvements](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/performance#improved-performance) , ensure that your tests are running in one of these improved instance configurations.

## Zonal and regional failure protection

When running your workloads in production, it is important to provision enough compute capacity to continue to serve your traffic in the event of the loss of an entire zone (for regional instances) or an entire region (for dual-region and multi-region instances). For more information about the recommended maximum CPU, see [alerts for high CPU utilization](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/cpu-utilization#recommended-max) .

## What's next

- Learn how to [design a Spanner schema](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/schema-design) .
- Find out how to [monitor Spanner performance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/monitoring-console) .
- Learn how to [troubleshoot issues with Key Visualizer](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/key-visualizer) .
- Learn about [Spanner pricing](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/pricing) .

documents.content:
> **PostgreSQL interface note:** The examples in this topic are intended for GoogleSQL-dialect databases.

## Overview

This page explains the concepts behind query execution plans and how Spanner uses them to perform queries in a distributed environment. To learn how to retrieve an execution plan for a specific query using the Google Cloud console, see [Understand how Spanner executes queries](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/sql-best-practices#how-execute-queries) . You can also view sampled historical query plans to compare query performance over time. To learn more, see [Sampled query plans](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-plans#sampled-plans) .

Spanner uses declarative SQL statements to query its databases. SQL statements define *what* the user wants without specifying *how* to obtain the results. A *query execution plan* is the set of steps for how the results are obtained. For a given SQL statement, there may be multiple ways to obtain the results. The Spanner query optimizer evaluates different execution plans and chooses the most efficient one. Spanner then uses the execution plan to retrieve the results. Execution plans support GoogleSQL-dialect databases and PostgreSQL-dialect databases.

For more information about the query optimizer, see [Query optimizer overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-optimizer/overview) .

Conceptually, an execution plan is a tree of relational operators. Each operator reads rows from its inputs and produces output rows. The result of the operator at the root of the execution is returned as the result of the SQL query.

As an example, consider the following query:

```
SELECT s.SongName FROM Songs AS s;
```

This query results in a query execution plan that can be visualized as:

![Example query execution plan](https://docs.cloud.google.com/static/spanner/docs/images/query-execution-1.png)

In this example, Spanner executes the query plan top-down, and data flows bottom-up. The [`distributed union`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-operators-distributed#distributed-union) operator executes first. The dashed blue lines indicate that this operator can make a remote call. Whether locally or remotely, it invokes the [`serialize result`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-operators-unary#serialize_result) operator and continues down the tree. When the [`table scan`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-operators-leaf#scan) operator produces a row, it immediately returns control to the `serialize result` operator. This process continues until the query scans all rows.

The queries and execution plans on this page are based on the following database schema:

```
CREATE TABLE Singers (
  SingerId   INT64 NOT NULL,
  FirstName  STRING(1024),
  LastName   STRING(1024),
  SingerInfo BYTES(MAX),
  BirthDate  DATE
) PRIMARY KEY(SingerId);

CREATE INDEX SingersByFirstLastName ON Singers(FirstName, LastName);

CREATE TABLE Albums (
  SingerId        INT64 NOT NULL,
  AlbumId         INT64 NOT NULL,
  AlbumTitle      STRING(MAX),
  MarketingBudget INT64
) PRIMARY KEY(SingerId, AlbumId),
  INTERLEAVE IN PARENT Singers ON DELETE CASCADE;

CREATE INDEX AlbumsByAlbumTitle ON Albums(AlbumTitle);

CREATE INDEX AlbumsByAlbumTitle2 ON Albums(AlbumTitle) STORING (MarketingBudget);

CREATE TABLE Songs (
  SingerId  INT64 NOT NULL,
  AlbumId   INT64 NOT NULL,
  TrackId   INT64 NOT NULL,
  SongName  STRING(MAX),
  Duration  INT64,
  SongGenre STRING(25)
) PRIMARY KEY(SingerId, AlbumId, TrackId),
  INTERLEAVE IN PARENT Albums ON DELETE CASCADE;

CREATE INDEX SongsBySingerAlbumSongNameDesc ON Songs(SingerId, AlbumId, SongName DESC), INTERLEAVE IN Albums;

CREATE INDEX SongsBySongName ON Songs(SongName);

CREATE TABLE Concerts (
  VenueId      INT64 NOT NULL,
  SingerId     INT64 NOT NULL,
  ConcertDate  DATE NOT NULL,
  BeginTime    TIMESTAMP,
  EndTime      TIMESTAMP,
  TicketPrices ARRAY<INT64>
) PRIMARY KEY(VenueId, SingerId, ConcertDate);
```

You can use the following Data Manipulation Language (DML) statements to add data to these tables:

```
INSERT INTO Singers (SingerId, FirstName, LastName, BirthDate)
VALUES (1, "Marc", "Richards", "1970-09-03"),
       (2, "Catalina", "Smith", "1990-08-17"),
       (3, "Alice", "Trentor", "1991-10-02"),
       (4, "Lea", "Martin", "1991-11-09"),
       (5, "David", "Lomond", "1977-01-29");

INSERT INTO Albums (SingerId, AlbumId, AlbumTitle)
VALUES (1, 1, "Total Junk"),
       (1, 2, "Go, Go, Go"),
       (2, 1, "Green"),
       (2, 2, "Forever Hold Your Peace"),
       (2, 3, "Terrified"),
       (3, 1, "Nothing To Do With Me"),
       (4, 1, "Play");

INSERT INTO Songs (SingerId, AlbumId, TrackId, SongName, Duration, SongGenre)
VALUES (2, 1, 1, "Let's Get Back Together", 182, "COUNTRY"),
       (2, 1, 2, "Starting Again", 156, "ROCK"),
       (2, 1, 3, "I Knew You Were Magic", 294, "BLUES"),
       (2, 1, 4, "42", 185, "CLASSICAL"),
       (2, 1, 5, "Blue", 238, "BLUES"),
       (2, 1, 6, "Nothing Is The Same", 303, "BLUES"),
       (2, 1, 7, "The Second Time", 255, "ROCK"),
       (2, 3, 1, "Fight Story", 194, "ROCK"),
       (3, 1, 1, "Not About The Guitar", 278, "BLUES");
```

> **Note:** You can run queries and retrieve execution plans even if the tables have no data.

Obtaining efficient execution plans is challenging because Spanner divides data into [*splits*](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/schema-and-data-model#database-splits) . Splits can move independently from each other, and Spanner can assign them to different servers, which might be in different physical locations. To evaluate execution plans over distributed data, Spanner performs the following tasks:

- Runs *subplans* locally on servers that store the data.
- Orchestrates and aggregates multiple remote executions with aggressive distribution pruning.

To enable this model, Spanner uses the [`distributed union`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-operators#distributed-union) operator, along with its [`distributed cross apply`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-operators#distributed-cross-apply) and [`distributed outer apply`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-operators#distributed-outer-apply) variants.

## How Spanner executes queries

Conceptually, query execution flows from top to bottom, and query results flow from bottom to top. The following diagram shows this pattern:

![Conceptual query plan](https://docs.cloud.google.com/static/spanner/docs/images/conceptual_query_plan.svg)

Spanner compiles a SQL query into an execution plan. To minimize the number of hops to the queried data, Spanner chooses an initial *root* server and sends the plan to this server. The root server performs the following actions:

- Initiates the remote execution of subplans, if necessary.
- Waits for results from the remote executions.
- Handles any remaining local execution steps, such as aggregating results.
- Returns the query results.

A remote server that receives a subplan acts as a root server for its subplan, following the same model as the topmost root server. This execution model results in a tree of remote executions.

## Key performance metrics

The Spanner Studio query plan visualizer displays summary metrics for query execution. Summary metrics represent the aggregate of metrics from all individual operators executed during the query. The following table describes the key performance metrics:

| Metric             | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|--------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Total elapsed time | The total wall-clock time taken to execute the query.                                                                                                                                                          |
| CPU time           | The total amount of CPU time spent across all servers involved in executing the query. Because some parts of query execution can proceed in parallel, the CPU time can be greater than the total elapsed time. |

## Sampled query plans

Spanner sampled query plans let you view samples of historical query plans and compare the performance of a query over time. Sampled query plans aren't available for all queries. Spanner might sample only queries that consume significant CPU. Spanner retains query plan samples for 30 days. To find query plan samples on the [Query insights](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/using-query-insights) page of the Google Cloud console, see [View sampled query plans](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/tune-query-with-visualizer#view-sampled-queries) .

The anatomy of a sampled query plan is the same as a regular query execution plan. For more information on how to understand visual plans and use them to debug your queries, see [A tour of the query plan visualizer](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/tune-query-with-visualizer#visual-plan-tour) .

### Common use cases for sampled query plans

Common use cases for sampled query plans include the following:

- Observing query plan changes because of [schema changes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/schema-updates) (for example, adding or removing an index).
- Observing query plan changes because of an [optimizer version update](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-optimizer/versions) .
- Observing query plan changes because of [new optimizer statistics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-optimizer/manage-query-optimizer#list-statistics-packages) . Spanner collects these statistics automatically every three days, or you can update them manually using the [`ANALYZE`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/standard-sql/data-definition-language#analyze-statistics) command.

If query performance varies significantly over time, or if you want to improve performance, then see [SQL best practices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/sql-best-practices) to construct optimized query statements that help Spanner find efficient execution plans.

## Common patterns

The following examples illustrate common patterns in Spanner execution plans.

### Aggregate queries

An aggregate query implements `GROUP BY` logic.

For example, the following query calculates song counts by singer:

```
SELECT s.SingerId, COUNT(*) AS SongCount
FROM Songs AS s
WHERE s.SingerId < 100
GROUP BY s.SingerId;
```

These are the results:

```
+----------+-----------+
| SingerId | SongCount |
+----------+-----------+
|        3 |         1 |
|        2 |         8 |
+----------+-----------+
```

Conceptually, this is the execution plan:

![Aggregate query execution plan](https://docs.cloud.google.com/static/spanner/docs/images/aggregate-query-plan.png)

Spanner sends the execution plan to a root server that coordinates the query execution and distributes subplans remotely.

This execution plan starts with a `distributed union` operator that distributes subplans to remote servers whose splits satisfy `SingerId < 100` . After the scan on individual splits completes, the `stream aggregate` operator aggregates rows to get the counts for each `SingerId` . The `serialize result` operator then serializes the result. Finally, the `distributed union` combines all results and returns the query results.

For more information about aggregates, see [Aggregate operators](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-operators#aggregate) .

### Co-located join queries

In [interleaved](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/schema-and-data-model#create-interleaved-tables) tables, Spanner physically stores related rows together. A *co-located join* is a join between interleaved tables. Co-located joins can improve performance compared to joins that require indexes or back joins.

For example, consider the following query:

```
SELECT al.AlbumTitle, so.SongName
FROM Albums AS al, Songs AS so
WHERE al.SingerId = so.SingerId AND
      al.AlbumId = so.AlbumId;
```

This query assumes that `Songs` is interleaved in `Albums` .

These are the results:

```
+-----------------------+--------------------------+
| AlbumTitle            | SongName                 |
+-----------------------+--------------------------+
| Nothing To Do With Me | Not About The Guitar     |
| Green                 | The Second Time          |
| Green                 | Starting Again           |
| Green                 | Nothing Is The Same      |
| Green                 | Let's Get Back Together  |
| Green                 | I Knew You Were Magic    |
| Green                 | Blue                     |
| Green                 | 42                       |
| Terrified             | Fight Story              |
+-----------------------+--------------------------+
```

This is the execution plan:

![Co-located join query execution plan](https://docs.cloud.google.com/static/spanner/docs/images/co-located-query-plan.png)

This execution plan starts with a `distributed union` operator that distributes subplans to remote servers, which contain splits of the `Albums` table. Because `Songs` is interleaved in `Albums` , each remote server executes the entire subplan locally without performing a join across different servers.

The subplans contain a `cross apply` operator. Each `cross apply` operator performs a [`table scan`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-operators#scan) on the `Albums` table to retrieve `SingerId` , `AlbumId` , and `AlbumTitle` . The `cross apply` operator then maps the output from the table scan to the output from an index scan on the `SongsBySingerAlbumSongNameDesc` index. This index is subject to a [filter](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-operators#filter) , which requires that the `SingerId` in the index matches the `SingerId` from the table scan output. Each `cross apply` operator sends its results to a [`serialize result`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-operators#serialize_result) operator, which serializes the `AlbumTitle` and `SongName` data and returns the results to the local distributed unions. The distributed union aggregates results from the local distributed unions and returns them as the query result.

### Index and back join queries

The previous example uses a join on two tables, where one table is interleaved in the other. If two tables, or a table and an index, aren't interleaved, then execution plans are more complex and less efficient.

Consider an index created with the following command:

```
CREATE INDEX SongsBySongName ON Songs(SongName);
```

To use this index in a query, select one of the following database dialect options:

### GoogleSQL

```
SELECT s.SongName, s.Duration
FROM Songs@{force_index=SongsBySongName} AS s
WHERE STARTS_WITH(s.SongName, "B");
```

### PostgreSQL

```
SELECT s.SongName, s.Duration
FROM Songs /*@ force_index=SongsBySongName */ AS s
WHERE STARTS_WITH(s.SongName, "B");
```

These are the results:

```
+----------+----------+
| SongName | Duration |
+----------+----------+
| Blue     |      238 |
+----------+----------+
```

This is the execution plan:

![Back join query execution plan](https://docs.cloud.google.com/static/spanner/docs/images/back-join-query-plan.png)

The resulting execution plan is complex because the `SongsBySongName` index doesn't contain the `Duration` column. To obtain the `Duration` value, Spanner back joins the indexed results to the `Songs` table. This is a join, but it isn't co-located because the `Songs` table and the `SongsBySongName` global index aren't interleaved. If data isn't co-located, then Spanner performs optimizations to speed up the execution. These optimizations make the execution plan more complex than the previous co-located join example.

The top operator is a `distributed cross apply` . The input side of this operator receives batches of rows from the `SongsBySongName` index that satisfy the `STARTS_WITH(s.SongName, "B")` predicate. The `distributed cross apply` operator then maps these batches to remote servers that contain splits with the `Duration` data. To retrieve the `Duration` column, the remote servers perform a table scan. This scan uses the `Condition:($Songs_key_TrackId' = $batched_Songs_key_TrackId)` filter condition, which joins `TrackId` from the `Songs` table to the `TrackId` columns of the rows batched from the `SongsBySongName` index.

Spanner aggregates the results into the final query answer. In turn, the input side of the `distributed cross apply` operator contains a `distributed union` or `local distributed union` pair to evaluate rows from the index that satisfy the `STARTS_WITH` predicate.

Consider a slightly different query that doesn't select the `s.Duration` column:

### GoogleSQL

```
SELECT s.SongName
FROM Songs@{force_index=SongsBySongName} AS s
WHERE STARTS_WITH(s.SongName, "B");
```

### PostgreSQL

```
SELECT s.SongName
FROM Songs /*@ force_index=SongsBySongName */ AS s
WHERE STARTS_WITH(s.SongName, "B");
```

The following execution plan shows that this query fully uses the index:

![Simpler query execution plan](https://docs.cloud.google.com/static/spanner/docs/images/index-query-plan.png)

The execution plan doesn't require a back join because the index contains all of the columns that the query requests.

### Understanding query distribution

The **Remote calls** statistic, found in the **Query** summary on the **Explanation** tab in the Console, reflects the number of calls made to other Spanner servers during query execution. While not a direct 1:1 count of unique data splits accessed, a higher number of remote calls often indicates that the query execution is more distributed, potentially spanning more servers and splits. This metric excludes calls within the same server. Monitoring this can help gauge the extent of query fanout.

### Sequential scan versus scattered seeks

Reading a contiguous range of rows is significantly faster than reading the same number of scattered rows.

For example, the following query sums the duration of songs from a specified set of singers. This query performs seeks for each specified singer ID. To see how many seeks the query performed, see the [Seek count](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-operators#scan) statistic.

```
SELECT SUM(Duration)
FROM Songs
WHERE SingerId IN (1, 3, 9, 10, 15);
```

However, if you structure the query to read a contiguous sequence of singer IDs, then you can improve performance by performing a sequential read of the `Songs` table. The `Songs` table contains `SingerId` as part of its primary key.

```
SELECT SUM(Duration)
FROM Songs
WHERE SingerId BETWEEN 1 AND 5;
```

This difference is relevant when you choose a join method and when you make schema design decisions, such as choosing a primary key. For more information about choosing a join method, see [How joins interact with scans](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-tuning#how-joins-interact-with-scans) .

### Sharing distributed unions

Every table or index in a query must have a corresponding distributed operator. This operator is either `distributed union` or a `distributed apply` . If two tables or indexes are interleaved in the same parent, then the query optimizer might use a single `distributed union` operator for both tables or indexes.

## What's next

- Learn about [query execution operators](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-operators) .
- Learn about the Spanner [query optimizer](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-optimizer/overview) .
- Learn how to [manage the query optimizer](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-optimizer/manage-query-optimizer) .

documents.content:
This page describes the key components of the query plan visualizer.

The query plan visualizer in Google Cloud console helps you understand the structure of the execution plan that Spanner chooses to evaluate a query.

The visualizer displays the plan as a visual graph, making it easier to analyze how Spanner executes your queries and identify potential performance bottlenecks. You can use the query plan visualizer to do any of the following:

- **Debug slow queries** : pinpoint which part of the query plan takes the most time or resources.
- **Validate optimizations** : compare query plans before and after making changes (like adding an index or rewriting a join) to verify improvements.
- **Understand query behavior** : learn how Spanner processes complex SQL statements, including joins, aggregations, and distributed operations.

## Benefits of using the query plan visualizer

Query plans can be complex. The visualizer simplifies analyzing plans by providing the following features:

- **Graphical representation** : displays the flow of data from tables and indexes through various operators to the final result.
- **Performance insights** : identifies expensive operators with visual cues for high latency and CPU consumption.
- **Row count visualization** : shows data volume at each step with line thickness indicators.
- **Detailed statistics** : provides specific runtime statistics for each operator.

## Access the query plan visualizer

You can access the query plan visualizer in the Google Cloud console through either of the following methods:

- **[Spanner Studio](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-plan-visualizer-overview#access-spanner-studio)** : generate a live, on-demand query plan while writing and testing queries.
- **[Query insights](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-plan-visualizer-overview#access-query-insights)** : view historical, sampled query plans captured from production workloads over time.

### View an on-demand plan in Spanner Studio

To view a query plan on-demand for a query in Spanner Studio:

1.  In the Google Cloud console, go to the Spanner **Instances** page.

2.  Click the name of the instance containing the database you want to query.

3.  In the **Databases** list, click the name of your database.

4.  In the navigation menu, click **Spanner Studio** .

5.  In the editor pane, enter your SQL query.

6.  Click **Run** .

7.  Click the **Explanation** tab.

### View a sampled plan in Query insights

To view a historical, sampled query plan in [Query insights](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/using-query-insights) :

1.  In the Google Cloud console, go to the Spanner **Instances** page.

2.  Click the name of the instance containing the database you want to investigate.

3.  In the navigation menu, click **Query insights** .

4.  Select the database and time range you want to analyze.

5.  In the **TopN queries** table, click the query or request tag you want to inspect.

6.  In the **Query plans samples** graph, click a sample dot representing a query execution.

7.  In the **Query plan visualizer** section, view the visual execution plan.

### Navigate the visualizer

The visualizer displays the query plan as a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

![Annotated query plan visualizer](https://docs.cloud.google.com/static/spanner/docs/images/query-plan-visualizer-color.png)

The query plan visualization might be large, depending on the query you executed. To hide or show details, click the **Expanded/Compact** view selector. To zoom in or out, use the zoom control.

The visualizer interface provides the following information panels:

- [Query summary](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-plan-visualizer-overview#query-summary)
- [Query execution timeline](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-plan-visualizer-overview#query-execution-timeline)

To download the visualized query plan, click **Download JSON** . To view the query plan at a later time, you can import the downloaded JSON profile back into Spanner Studio. If you need to troubleshoot performance issues, then share the JSON file with the Spanner support team.

## Query plan acyclic graph

The logic that Spanner uses to run the query appears as a DAG. The graph displays data flow from the bottom up. Tables and indexes appear at the bottom, and the final query output appears at the top.

Each node in the graph is represented by a card. Each card represents an iterator that consumes rows from its inputs and produces rows for its parent.

Lines that connect the cards represent the flow of rows between iterators. The line thickness indicates the relative number of rows passed. Thicker lines indicate more rows.

Each card on the graph contains the following information:

- **Iterator name** : the name of the iterator.
- **Runtime statistics** : the number of rows returned, the latency, and the CPU usage.

Click a card to view more information about the latency, CPU usage, rows returned, execution count, and machine group count.

For more information about operators, see [Query execution operators](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-operators) .

Spanner queries often retrieve data from multiple database splits. A **machine group** represents a set of contiguous query execution operators that execute together for a set of splits. Within a single machine group, operators execute sequentially from the bottom up, whereas different machine groups execute in parallel. When data moves between splits across machine group boundaries, it travels through remote procedure calls (RPCs).

For more information about splits, see [Database splits](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/schema-and-data-model#database-splits) .

The visualizer helps you distinguish between logical and physical distribution:

- **Logical boundaries** : Cards labeled **Distributed** indicate where the query planner split the query logic.
- **Physical distribution** : The machine group colors on the graph represent actual physical execution derived from runtime statistics.

Physical boundaries often align with logical distributed operators, but they can differ depending on how splits are placed across servers.

## Query summary

The **Query summary** pane provides the following high-level execution metrics and highlights potential bottlenecks in the query:

- **Total elapsed time** : the total time taken to run the query from start to finish.
- **CPU time** : the cumulative CPU time consumed across all threads and servers processing the query.
- **Plan creation time** : the time the query compiler and optimizer spent generating the execution plan.
- **Server queue delay** : the duration the query spent waiting in server queues before processing began.
- **Rows returned** : the total number of rows returned in the final query result.
- **Rows scanned** : the total number of rows read from storage across all scanned tables and indexes.
- **Remote calls** : the total number of RPCs made between splits or machine groups.
- **Query optimizer version** : the version of the Spanner query optimizer used to compile the plan.
- **Statistics package** : the optimizer statistics package used for cost-based optimization.

### Prominent operators

The **Prominent operators** section highlights the most resource-intensive iterators in the query plan:

- **Highest latency** : the operator with the longest execution duration.
- **Highest CPU time** : the operator that consumed the most CPU time.
- **Highest row count** : the operator that processed or returned the most rows.

## Query execution timeline

The **Query execution timeline** tab displays a time-based graph that shows how long each machine group executes its portion of the query. A machine group might not run for the entire query duration, or it might run multiple times. However, the timeline displays only the start time of its initial execution and the end time of its final execution.

## Visual cues for performance

The visualizer uses the following colors and icons to help you spot issues:

- **Red bars** : indicate the percentage of latency or CPU time consumed by that operator relative to the total query.
- **Warning triangles** : indicate that a full table scan occurred. Such scans often suggest an opportunity to optimize the query, for example, by adding a secondary index.
- **Machine group colors** : differentiate machine groups and highlight transitions between groups. These transitions require remote execution across different machines, which incurs serialization and network overhead. The query execution timeline also displays these machine group colors.

## What's next

- Learn how to [tune a query using the query plan visualizer](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/tune-query-with-visualizer) .
- Read about specific [Query execution operators](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-operators) .
- Understand [Query execution plans](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-plans) in depth.

This page describes techniques for tuning Spanner query performance. Before you begin tuning your queries, review the following pages, which explain foundational concepts and tools used in query tuning:

- [SQL best practices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/sql-best-practices)

## Benchmark recommendations

The most reliable performance statistics come from running a load test that uses different, randomized query parameter values from a Google Cloud virtual machine (VM) instance that resides in the same region as the target instance.

Avoid relying on the Spanner Studio or the `QueryMode.PROFILE` mode to benchmark queries, because these tools don't replicate actual production network and client environments. However, after a load test identifies a performance issue, query plans (whether sampled in Query insights or run on demand in the Spanner Studio) are useful tools for investigating that specific issue.

## Understand query execution plans

In the query plan visualizer, a query execution plan is shown as a tree of operators, where each operator reads rows from its child operators, processes them, and passes the results up to its parent operator.

For most operators in the visual plan, the reported latency is additive (it reflects only the time spent in that operator). However, for the `Distributed union` and `Distributed apply` operators, the reported latency is cumulative: it includes both the time spent in the distributed operator itself and the time spent in its child operators. For more information about these operators, see [Distributed union](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-operators-distributed#distributed-union) and [Distributed apply](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-operators-distributed#distributed-apply) .

For example, in the following distributed union plan, the `Distributed union` card reports a total latency of 8.46 ms, while its child `Stream aggregate` operator reports 3.51 ms and `Table scan` reports 1 ms. Because the `Distributed union` latency is cumulative, the `Distributed union` operator itself adds only about 5 ms of latency, rather than 8 ms:

![A distributed union execution plan with cumulative latency.](https://docs.cloud.google.com/static/spanner/docs/images/distribution_cumulative_latency_1.png)

In the next example, the `Distributed union` card reports 13.69 ms of latency, while its child operators ( `Stream aggregate` at \<1 ms, `Cross apply` at 1.14 ms, `Table scan` on `Albums` at \<1 ms, `Filter scan` at 1 ms, and `Table scan` on `Singers` at 10.85 ms) account for approximately 13 ms. As a result, the `Distributed union` operator itself adds less than 1 ms of latency, rather than 13 ms:

![A second distributed union execution plan with cumulative latency.](https://docs.cloud.google.com/static/spanner/docs/images/distribution_cumulative_latency_2.png)

You can also view the cumulative latency values in the operator summary panel.

## Combine multiple indexes

When a query filters on multiple indexed columns using `OR` or `AND` conditions, Spanner can sometimes combine multiple secondary indexes to avoid scanning the full base table. The examples in this section extend the `Albums` table from the preceding example schema by adding a `ReleaseDate` column and an `AlbumsByReleaseDate` secondary index:

```
CREATE TABLE Albums (
  SingerId        INT64 NOT NULL,
  AlbumId         INT64 NOT NULL,
  AlbumTitle      STRING(MAX),
  ReleaseDate     DATE,
  MarketingBudget INT64
) PRIMARY KEY(SingerId, AlbumId),
  INTERLEAVE IN PARENT Singers ON DELETE CASCADE;

CREATE INDEX AlbumsByAlbumTitle ON Albums(AlbumTitle);

CREATE INDEX AlbumsByReleaseDate ON Albums(ReleaseDate);
```

Consider the following query, which uses an `OR` condition to filter on predicates from two separate secondary indexes ( `AlbumsByAlbumTitle` and `AlbumsByReleaseDate` ):

```
SELECT a.AlbumId, a.AlbumTitle, a.ReleaseDate
FROM Albums AS a
WHERE a.AlbumTitle = 'Play' OR a.ReleaseDate = '2023-09-07';
```

When a query has an `OR` condition on predicates from two separate indexes, Spanner might use cost-based optimization to read both indexes and combine the results (an index union). You can also force this optimization by adding the `INDEX_STRATEGY=FORCE_INDEX_UNION` table hint to the query:

```
SELECT a.AlbumId, a.AlbumTitle, a.ReleaseDate
FROM Albums@{INDEX_STRATEGY=FORCE_INDEX_UNION} AS a
WHERE a.AlbumTitle = 'Play' OR a.ReleaseDate = '2023-09-07';
```

For more information about table hints, see [Table hints](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax#table_hints) .

The following execution plan diagram shows how Spanner evaluates this `OR` condition (disjunction) by scanning each branch separately and combining the results using the `Union all` and `Hash aggregate` operators:

![An index disjunction execution plan.](https://docs.cloud.google.com/static/spanner/docs/images/index-union-rewrite.png)

Next, consider a query that uses an `AND` condition to filter on both indexed columns:

```
SELECT a.AlbumId, a.ReleaseDate, a.AlbumTitle
FROM Albums AS a
WHERE a.AlbumTitle = 'Aardvark' AND a.ReleaseDate = '2023-09-07';
```

With an `AND` condition, Spanner picks a single index by default and then joins back to the base table, if needed, to evaluate the remaining condition in the `AND` clause. To determine whether this base table back-join is a performance bottleneck, inspect the query execution plan in the visualizer: if the `Index scan` operator returns many rows that are subsequently filtered out after joining with the `Table scan` operator on the base table (resulting in high latency or CPU time on the `Table scan` branch relative to the final number of rows returned), then the back-join is a bottleneck.

If the base table back-join is the bottleneck for the query, the recommended solution is to add the extra column in the `AND` condition to the `STORING` clause of the secondary index so Spanner can evaluate both conditions directly from the index without reading the base table:

```
CREATE INDEX AlbumsByAlbumTitleStoringReleaseDate
  ON Albums(AlbumTitle)
  STORING (ReleaseDate);
```

If modifying the index isn't viable, an alternative is to rewrite the query to perform an intersection of both indexes using `INTERSECT DISTINCT` , and then join the matching primary keys back to the `Albums` base table:

```
SELECT union_a.AlbumId, a.ReleaseDate, a.AlbumTitle FROM
  (SELECT a1.SingerId, a1.AlbumId
  FROM Albums @{force_index=AlbumsByReleaseDate} AS a1
  WHERE a1.ReleaseDate = '2023-09-07'
  INTERSECT DISTINCT
  SELECT a2.SingerId, a2.AlbumId
  FROM Albums @{force_index=AlbumsByAlbumTitle} AS a2
  WHERE a2.AlbumTitle = 'Aardvark') AS union_a
JOIN Albums AS a
  ON a.SingerId = union_a.SingerId AND a.AlbumId = union_a.AlbumId;
```

The following execution plan diagram shows the rewritten query. Notice how the plan uses two `Index scan` operators ( `on AlbumsByAlbumTitle` and `on AlbumsByReleaseDate` ) to find the intersecting keys before performing the `Table scan` on the `Albums` base table:

![An index conjunction execution plan.](https://docs.cloud.google.com/static/spanner/docs/images/index-conjunction-rewrite.png)

If filtering across multiple columns is a frequent pattern in your workload, consider using multi-column full-text search instead of secondary indexes. For more information, see [Perform a multi-column search](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/full-text-search/search-multiple-columns#perform_a_multi-column_search) .

## Optimize joins

When Spanner executes a query that joins multiple tables, the query optimizer chooses both the *join order* (the sequence in which tables are joined) and the *join method* (the algorithm used to combine rows from two inputs, such as an apply join, hash join, or merge join). If a query with a join is slower than expected, you can use a query hint to instruct Spanner to use a different join order or join method. This changes the execution plan, but doesn't change the returned results. For example:

### GoogleSQL

Force join order:

```
SELECT *
FROM Singers AS s JOIN@{FORCE_JOIN_ORDER=TRUE} Albums AS a
ON s.SingerId = a.SingerId
WHERE s.LastName LIKE '%x%' AND a.AlbumTitle LIKE '%love%';
```

Change join method:

```
SELECT *
FROM Singers AS s JOIN@{JOIN_METHOD=HASH_JOIN} Albums AS a
ON s.SingerId = a.SingerId;
```

### PostgreSQL

Force join order:

```
SELECT *
FROM Singers AS s JOIN/*@ FORCE_JOIN_ORDER=TRUE */ Albums AS a
ON s.SingerId = a.SingerId
WHERE s.LastName LIKE '%x%' AND a.AlbumTitle LIKE '%love%';
```

Change join method:

```
SELECT *
FROM Singers AS s JOIN/*@ JOIN_METHOD=HASH_JOIN */ Albums AS a
ON s.SingerId = a.SingerId;
```

The following sections provide background that can help you determine which join orders and join methods can help improve query performance.

### Join method and scans

Spanner supports several join methods, and your choice of join method directly affects how Spanner scans the underlying tables or indexes:

- **Apply join** (known in some systems as a lookup join or nested loop join): executes its right-hand ("map") side once for each row from the left-hand ("input") side. Because each right-hand lookup uses values from the current left-hand row, the *join columns from the left can be used as a seek key on the right* . A *distributed apply join* works similarly to a local apply join, but batches rows together for more efficient communication across splits in a distributed join.
- **Hash join** : reads rows from one input to build an in-memory hash table on the join keys, and then scans the other input to probe the hash table for matches.
- **Merge join** : reads both inputs in sorted order on the join keys and merges matching rows in a single pass.

For example, consider the following query that joins `Singers` and `Albums` :

```
SELECT s.*, a.AlbumTitle
FROM Singers AS s
JOIN Albums AS a ON s.SingerId = a.SingerId
WHERE s.SingerId = 2 AND a.AlbumId = 1;
```

With an apply join, `s.SingerId = a.SingerId` acts as a seek condition on the right side of the join, so the query only has to read one row from the `Albums` table.

By contrast, in a hash join or merge join, the left and right inputs are read independently of each other, so the join condition doesn't provide a seek key from one side to the other. In the worst case, a hash or merge join performs a full-table scan of each input.

In interactive and transactional queries, most joins use indexes, so distributed apply is the most common join type in Spanner. However, sometimes a hash or merge join is a better choice because reading a contiguous range of rows is significantly faster than performing the same number of scattered single-row seeks. The tradeoff is whether it's faster to seek fewer rows (using an apply join) or scan a larger contiguous range of rows (using a hash or merge join). For more information about this tradeoff, see [Sequential reads versus scattered seeks](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-plans#sequential-reads-vs-scattered-seeks) .

For queries that read thousands of rows, if an index is available on the join key, it's usually safer to use a distributed apply join. This is because the apply join cost is proportional to the number of joined rows, whereas with a hash or merge join, the cost can be proportional to the total table size. For larger queries (such as queries that process millions of rows), using a hash or merge join might offer a significant performance improvement.

For more information about join operators and hints, see the following resources:

- [Apply join](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-operators-binary#apply-join)
- [Distributed apply](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-operators-distributed#distributed-apply)
- [Hash join](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-operators-binary#hash-join)
- [Merge join](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-operators-binary#merge-join)
- [Join methods reference](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax#join_methods)

### Join ordering

As in other relational database management systems (RDBMSs), order joins to keep the intermediate result size as small as possible. That means filtering out data as early as possible, and deferring any large matches as late as possible.

If you provide the `FORCE_JOIN_ORDER=TRUE` hint, Spanner executes the joins in the exact order in which they appear in the query text. Move joins with very selective filters earlier in the query, and move joins with large matches later in the query.

## Optimize aggregations

The following techniques can help you reduce the number of rows scanned and sorted during aggregation queries.

### Retrieve one row per key prefix

A common aggregation pattern is to retrieve one row per key prefix (for example, the row with the highest version number or timestamp). In GoogleSQL, the most efficient way to do this is to use `ANY_VALUE` with `HAVING MAX` , which finds the row with the maximum value and returns the requested column in a single aggregation pass without requiring a self-join or full sort. For example, the following query groups the `Concerts` table by `ConcertDate` and returns the `BeginTime` of the concert with the latest `EndTime` for each date:

```
SELECT ConcertDate, ANY_VALUE(BeginTime HAVING MAX(EndTime))
FROM Concerts
GROUP BY ConcertDate;
```

### Check row existence

To check whether a table has any rows, or rows that match a specific condition, use `LIMIT` rather than `COUNT` . For example:

```
SELECT 1 FROM Albums LIMIT 1;
```

## Increase parallelism

Spanner divides tables and indexes into contiguous primary-key ranges called *splits* , which can be processed in parallel across multiple servers. Typically, Spanner chooses query parallelism to balance latency and efficiency. For example, if a query has a `LIMIT` clause, it might use less parallelism to avoid wasting work that the limit discards. The number of splits scanned by the query limits the maximum degree of parallelism.

For queries with limits or large scans, you can set the `USE_ADDITIONAL_PARALLELISM=TRUE` statement hint to instruct Spanner to optimize primarily for latency:

### GoogleSQL

```
@{USE_ADDITIONAL_PARALLELISM=TRUE}
SELECT *
FROM Singers
LIMIT 10;
```

### PostgreSQL

```
/*@ USE_ADDITIONAL_PARALLELISM=TRUE */
SELECT *
FROM Singers
LIMIT 10;
```

This hint might saturate the CPU on a given split. If the query is long running, send it with medium request priority to avoid increasing latency for other high-priority queries.

## Optimize limits

If a query contains a `LIMIT` clause but scans many more rows than the limit value, check the following potential causes:

### Missing index

If a query has a filter that can't be satisfied by using an index, the query plan scans the base table or an index that doesn't provide the required sort order. The query then fully sorts the matching data before evaluating the `LIMIT` clause.

To resolve this issue, consider adding a secondary index that covers the filter columns. If the index is defined as `NULL_FILTERED` (meaning that it excludes rows where an indexed column is `NULL` ), make sure that the query predicate includes `IS NOT NULL` so the optimizer can use the index. For more information about creating secondary indexes, see [Secondary indexes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/secondary-indexes) .

### Full sort

If an index exists on the filtered column, but the index doesn't provide the sort order required by the `ORDER BY` clause, Spanner must read all matching rows and pass them to a `Sort` operator in the query execution plan before applying the `LIMIT` .

To avoid a full sort, specify the columns in your `CREATE INDEX` statement in the following order:

- First, any columns that have an equality ( `=` ) or `IN` condition in the query
- Then, the same columns as the query's `ORDER BY` clause, in the same order, and with the same sort direction ( `ASC` or `DESC` )

For example, suppose you have a `Users` table (not shown in the preceding example schema) and want to optimize the following query:

```
SELECT * FROM Users
WHERE Name='Alex'
ORDER BY LastLogin DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Create an index on `(Name, LastLogin DESC)` so Spanner can read the top 10 rows directly in index order without sorting:

```
CREATE INDEX UsersByNameLastLogin ON Users(Name, LastLogin DESC);
```

### Order by key suffix

Even when an index includes the `ORDER BY` column as a suffix of the index key, a query might still scan extra rows if there is an `IN` , `OR` , or range predicate on one of the prefix columns of the index.

For example, consider the following query that uses the `(Name, LastLogin DESC)` index from the preceding full sort example, which isn't part of the example schema:

```
SELECT *
FROM Users
WHERE Name IN ('Alex','Amal')
ORDER BY LastLogin DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Because `Name` matches multiple values, the matching rows aren't stored in a single globally sorted range by `LastLogin DESC` . You can restructure the query using `UNNEST` and a join so Spanner retrieves the top rows for each `Name` value separately and then combines them:

```
SELECT *
FROM UNNEST(['Alex','Amal']) AS Name
JOIN Users AS u ON u.Name = Name
ORDER BY LastLogin DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

This rewrite results in more efficient scans by reading the minimum number of rows from each bound prefix key ( `'Alex'` and `'Amal'` ), followed by a small sort over the combined results to produce the final `LIMIT` .

A common special case of this pattern is a shard prefix, where a `ShardId` column is added as the leading key column to distribute writes across splits. For example, the following query scans across 32 shards ( `0` through `31` ):

```
SELECT *
FROM Users
WHERE ShardId BETWEEN 0 AND 31
ORDER BY LastLogin DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

To optimize this query, explicitly enumerate the shard IDs ( `0` through `31` ) and join them against the `Users` table using `GENERATE_ARRAY` in GoogleSQL or `generate_series` in PostgreSQL:

### GoogleSQL

```
SELECT *
FROM GENERATE_ARRAY(0, 31) AS id
JOIN Users AS u ON u.ShardId = id
ORDER BY LastLogin DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

### PostgreSQL

```
SELECT *
FROM generate_series(0, 31) AS id
JOIN Users AS u ON u.ShardId = id
ORDER BY LastLogin DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

For more information about these array and series generation functions, see [`GENERATE_ARRAY`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/standard-sql/array_functions#generate_array) for GoogleSQL and [`generate_series`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/postgresql/functions) for PostgreSQL.

## Understand scan performance

The following sections describe the most common causes of slow table or index scans and how to mitigate them.

### Deleted rows

By default, Spanner retains deleted or overwritten rows for one hour to support historical reads and point-in-time recovery, and you can increase this retention period up to seven days. After an old row version passes the retention period, it becomes eligible for removal during background storage compaction, which can take up to seven more days. Until an old row version is compacted, queries that scan the key range might have to read the deleted or overwritten row versions and filter them out. For more information about data retention, see [Point-in-time recovery (PITR)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/pitr) .

You can check whether a query scanned deleted rows by inspecting the **Deleted rows scanned** metric in the **Scan** operator details view in the query plan visualizer details panel.

To mitigate slow scans caused by a large number of recently deleted rows, you can trigger a manual data compaction. For more information, see [Manual data compaction](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/manual-data-compaction) .

### Large rows

For small rows (up to a few hundred bytes), the cost of a scan depends primarily on the number of rows scanned. As row size increases, the byte size of the rows becomes more significant. In row-oriented storage, the total size of the row affects scan performance, not just the size of the columns projected by the query.

For scan-heavy analytical queries over large tables, consider using the columnar engine. For more information, see [Monitor columnar engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/monitor-columnar-engine) .

For queries on narrower sets of rows, if a table has both large columns and smaller columns that are frequently queried, consider the following options:

- Separate the larger columns into a non-default locality group (which stores specified columns separately on disk from the rest of the table) or a separate child table so scans of the smaller columns don't read the large column data. For more information, see [Create and manage locality groups](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/create-manage-locality-groups) .
- For additional read-time optimization, duplicate the smaller columns into a secondary index with the same primary key as the base table, using the `STORING` clause to include the smaller columns.

For example, suppose a `Documents` table (not part of the preceding example schema) stores a small `Metadata` string alongside a large `Content` JSON object. You can create a secondary index that stores only `Metadata` so queries that don't need `Content` can scan the smaller index instead of the base table:

```
CREATE TABLE Documents (
  Id INT64,
  Metadata STRING(MAX),
  Content JSON
) PRIMARY KEY (Id);

CREATE INDEX DocumentMetadata ON Documents(Id) STORING (Metadata);
```

### Large interleaved data

When tables are interleaved, Spanner physically stores each parent row together with its interleaved child rows in key order. If a parent table has many interleaved child rows, or a child table has significantly fewer rows than its parent or sibling tables, then range scans over the smaller table are sparser and less efficient because the scan must skip over the interleaved rows from the other tables.

For example, consider the following schema (not part of the preceding example schema), in which both `Transaction` and `AuthorizedPerson` are interleaved in `Account` :

```
CREATE TABLE Account (
  AccountId INT64,
  -- Additional columns omitted
) PRIMARY KEY (AccountId);

CREATE TABLE Transaction (
  AccountId INT64,
  TransactionId STRING(MAX),
  -- Additional columns omitted
) PRIMARY KEY (AccountId, TransactionId),
INTERLEAVE IN PARENT Account;

CREATE TABLE AuthorizedPerson (
  AccountId INT64,
  SignerId INT64,
  Name STRING(MAX),
  -- Additional columns omitted
) PRIMARY KEY (AccountId, SignerId),
INTERLEAVE IN PARENT Account;
```

If every `Account` row has thousands of `Transaction` rows and only a few `AuthorizedPerson` rows, a range scan on `Account` or `AuthorizedPerson` has a higher per-row cost than a range scan on `Transaction` (even though its total cost is still lower). This happens because a `Transaction` scan reads many contiguous `Transaction` rows at once, whereas a scan on `Account` or `AuthorizedPerson` has fewer adjacent rows of the same table and must skip over the interleaved `Transaction` rows.

To optimize range scans on the sparser table ( `Account` or `AuthorizedPerson` ), create a non-interleaved secondary index that duplicates the columns needed by your query, similar to the approach for large rows:

```
CREATE INDEX AuthorizedPersonByAccount
  ON AuthorizedPerson(AccountId, SignerId)
  STORING (Name);
```

## Use batch-oriented execution

Spanner can execute query scans and query operators using either a row-oriented method (processing one row at a time) or a batch-oriented method (processing blocks of rows at a time). The following sections explain how to inspect and configure batch-oriented scans and batch-oriented operator execution.

### Batch-oriented scans

Certain Spanner queries might benefit from using a batch-oriented processing method when scanning data rather than the more common row-oriented processing method. Processing scans in batches is a more efficient way to process large volumes of data all at once, and it lets queries achieve lower CPU utilization and latency.

The Spanner scan operation always starts execution in the row-oriented method. During this time, Spanner collects several runtime metrics. Then, Spanner applies a set of heuristics based on the result of these metrics to determine the optimal scan method. When appropriate, Spanner switches to a batch-oriented processing method to help improve scan throughput and performance.

#### Common use cases

Queries with the following characteristics generally benefit from batch-oriented processing:

- Large scans over infrequently updated data
- Scans with predicates on fixed-width columns
- Scans with large seek counts (a seek uses an index to retrieve records)

#### Use cases without performance gains

Not all queries benefit from batch-oriented processing. The following query types perform better with row-oriented scan processing:

- **Point lookup queries** : queries that fetch only one row.
- **Small scan queries** : table scans that scan only a few rows, unless they have large seek counts.
- **Queries with a `LIMIT` clause** : queries that stop scanning after returning a fixed number of rows.
- **Queries that read high-churn data** : queries in which more than approximately 10% of the data read is frequently updated.
- **Queries with rows containing large values** : queries on rows that contain values larger than 32,000 bytes (pre-compression) in a single column.

#### Check the scan method used by a query

To check whether your query uses batch-oriented processing, row-oriented processing, or automatically switches between the two scan methods, follow these steps:

1.  In the Google Cloud console, go to the Spanner **Instances** page.

2.  Click the name of the instance with the query that you want to investigate.

3.  In the **Databases** table, click the database with the query that you want to investigate.

4.  In the Spanner navigation menu, click **Spanner Studio** .

5.  Click add **New SQL editor tab** or add **New tab** .

6.  In the query editor, enter your query.

7.  Click **Run** .

    Spanner runs the query and shows the results.

8.  In the query editor pane, click the **Explanation** tab.

    Spanner shows the query execution plan visualizer. Each card on the graph represents an iterator. For more information about execution plans, see [Query execution plans](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-plans) .

9.  Click the **Table scan** iterator card to open an information panel.

    The information panel shows contextual information about the selected scan, including the scan method ( **Method** ). **Automatic** indicates that Spanner determines the scanning method. Other possible values include **Batch** for batch-oriented processing and **Row** for row-oriented processing, as shown in the following image:

    ![A table scan card shows the scan method as Automatic.](https://docs.cloud.google.com/static/spanner/docs/images/automatic-table-scan.png)

#### Enforce the scan method used by a query

To optimize query performance, Spanner chooses the optimal scan method for your query. Google recommends that you use this default scan method. However, there might be scenarios in which you want to enforce a specific type of scan method.

##### Enforce batch-oriented scanning

You can enforce batch-oriented scanning at the table level and statement level.

To enforce the batch-oriented scan method at the table level, use a table hint in your query:

### GoogleSQL

```
SELECT *
FROM (Singers@{SCAN_METHOD=BATCH} AS s
  JOIN Albums AS a ON s.SingerId = a.SingerId);
```

### PostgreSQL

```
SELECT *
FROM (Singers/*@ scan_method=batch */ AS s
  JOIN Albums AS a ON s.SingerId = a.SingerId);
```

To enforce the batch-oriented scan method at the statement level, use a statement hint in your query:

### GoogleSQL

```
@{SCAN_METHOD=BATCH}
SELECT *
FROM Singers;
```

### PostgreSQL

```
/*@ scan_method=batch */
SELECT *
FROM Singers;
```

When you use a statement-level hint, it applies to the entire query. Setting the hint at the table level is preferable and provides more granular control.

##### Force row-oriented scanning

Although Google doesn't recommend disabling the automatic scanning method set by Spanner, you can disable it and use the row-oriented scanning method for troubleshooting purposes, such as diagnosing latency.

To disable the automatic scan method selection and enforce row processing at the table level, use a table hint in your query:

### GoogleSQL

```
SELECT *
FROM (Singers@{SCAN_METHOD=ROW} AS s
  JOIN Albums AS a ON s.SingerId = a.SingerId);
```

### PostgreSQL

```
SELECT *
FROM (Singers/*@ scan_method=row */ AS s
  JOIN Albums AS a ON s.SingerId = a.SingerId);
```

To disable the automatic scan method and enforce row processing at the statement level, use a statement hint in your query:

### GoogleSQL

```
@{SCAN_METHOD=ROW}
SELECT *
FROM Singers;
```

### PostgreSQL

```
/*@ scan_method=row */
SELECT *
FROM Singers;
```

### Execution method

In addition to batch-oriented scans, you can also optimize query execution by enforcing the execution method at the statement level. This only works for some operators, and it's independent of the scan method, which is only used by the scan operator. For more information about batch-oriented scans, see the [Batch-oriented scans](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-tuning#optimize-scans) section of this document.

By default, most operators execute in the row-oriented method, which processes data one row at a time. Vectorized operators execute in the batch-oriented method to help improve execution throughput and performance. These operators process data one block at a time. When an operator needs to process many rows, the batch-oriented execution method is usually more efficient.

#### Execution method versus scan method

The query execution method is independent of the query scan method. You can set one, both, or neither of these methods in your query hint.

The query execution method refers to the way query operators process intermediate results and how the operators interact with each other, whereas the scan method refers to the way the scan operator interacts with the Spanner storage layer.

#### Enforce the execution method used by the query

To optimize query performance, Spanner chooses the optimal execution method for your query based on various heuristics. Google recommends that you use this default execution method. However, there might be scenarios in which you want to enforce a specific type of execution method.

You can enforce your execution method at the statement level. The `EXECUTION_METHOD` query hint is advisory rather than a directive. Ultimately, the query optimizer decides which method to use for each individual operator.

To enforce the batch-oriented execution method at the statement level, use a statement hint in your query:

### GoogleSQL

```
@{EXECUTION_METHOD=BATCH}
SELECT *
FROM Singers;
```

### PostgreSQL

```
/*@ EXECUTION_METHOD=BATCH */
SELECT *
FROM Singers;
```

Although Google doesn't recommend disabling the automatic execution method set by Spanner, you can disable it and use the row-oriented execution method for troubleshooting purposes, such as diagnosing latency.

To disable the automatic execution method and enforce the row-oriented execution method at the statement level, use a statement hint in your query:

### GoogleSQL

```
@{EXECUTION_METHOD=ROW}
SELECT *
FROM Singers;
```

### PostgreSQL

```
/*@ EXECUTION_METHOD=ROW */
SELECT *
FROM Singers;
```

#### Check which execution method is enabled

Not all Spanner operators support both batch-oriented and row-oriented execution methods. For each operator, the query execution plan visualizer shows the execution method in the iterator card. If the execution method is batch-oriented, it shows **Batch** . If it's row-oriented, it shows **Row** . For more information about the visualizer, see [Query execution plans](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-execution-plans) .

If the operators in your query execute using different execution methods, the execution method adapters `DataBlockToRowAdapter` and `RowToDataBlockAdapter` appear between the operators to show the change in execution method. For more information about these operators, see [`DataBlockToRowAdapter`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-operators-unary#datablocktorowadapter) and [`RowToDataBlockAdapter`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/query-operators-unary#rowtodatablockadapter) .
